svg.title: Microscopy
svg.desc: Magnification & resolution: Magnification: how much larger the image is. Resolution: distinguish two nearby points as separate. A blurry photo can be enlarged without adding detail. Bigger does not mean clearer. Light & electron: Light microscopes show cells and visible structures. Electron microscopes have much greater magnification and resolving power → reveal finer sub-cellular detail. Better resolution separates nearby details. Size formulae: Magnification = image ÷ actual size. Actual = image ÷ magnification. Image = actual × magnification. Use the same units before dividing. Magnification has no unit; sizes do. Worked magnification: Image 30 mm; actual 60 µm. 30 × 1,000 = 30,000 µm. 30,000 ÷ 60 = ×500. Microscope total = eyepiece × objective: ×10 × ×40 = ×400. Drawing magnification depends on drawing size, not automatically the microscope setting. Units & standard form: 1 cm = 10 mm; 1 mm = 1,000 µm; 1 µm = 1,000 nm. 1 µm = 10⁻⁶ m; 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m. Large → small units: multiply; reverse: divide. a × 10ⁿ, 1 ≤ a < 10. Example: 0.000060 m = 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ m. Scale & area: 20 µm ÷ 2 µm = 10: one order of magnitude. Convert units before comparing. Scale bar = actual distance; compare image length with it. Estimate relative sizes/areas when boundaries are unclear. For similar shapes, length ×2 → area ×4; state this assumption. Prepare the slide: Observe plant and animal cells. Thin onion epidermis + water; suitable stain (e.g. iodine) improves contrast. Lower coverslip at an angle to reduce bubbles. Thin tissue lets light through and avoids overlap. Use prepared animal cells or samples approved by your teacher. Handle glass, stains and samples safely. Focus & draw: Lowest-power objective; coarse then fine focus. Centre cells; increase magnification; use fine focus. Draw clear pencil outlines, no shading. Label identifiable structures; add magnification scale or scale bar. Interpret visible features, not memory alone.
